notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • The triage framing this note picks a leg from — Simon Willison: the lethal trifecta for AI agents

  • Patterns with provable resistance, and what each costs in utility — Design patterns for securing LLM agents against prompt injections (arXiv 2506.08837)

  • The measured utility price of a by-design defence — Defeating prompt injections by design — CaMeL (arXiv 2503.18813)

0. 🔒 Owned Elsewhere

Concepts assumed (don't re-read unless rusty):

  • The lethal trifecta — the three-checkbox triage test.

  • prompt injection in agents — why the model can't separate data from instructions.

What this note adds: the choice. The trifecta tells you to break a leg; it doesn't say which, and each leg costs a different capability. This note prices the three, and shows the arithmetic for why hardening all three instead is not a fourth option.

1. 🎯 Recall Check

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
Cheapest leg to break, usually? Exfiltration — remove outbound channels, keep the rest.
What breaking the data leg costs? Answers about anything the agent can no longer see.
Why detection isn't a leg? It's probabilistic; d^n collapses over repeated attempts.
Measured price of a by-design defence? CaMeL: 77% of AgentDojo tasks solved vs 84% undefended.
When you can't break any leg? Then the deployment needs a human on every outbound action.

2. The Decision in 30 Seconds

The trifecta says any two legs are survivable and all three is exfiltration, so the design question is which one I remove. I reach for the exfiltration leg first, because it's usually the one the product needs least — no send, no post, no fetch-arbitrary-URL, and results render to a human who decides what leaves. Breaking the data leg costs capability directly, and breaking the untrusted-content leg is only available if the inputs can be enumerated, which for anything touching the open web they can't. What I won't do is claim a classifier as the answer: a filter that catches 99% of attempts still lets one through within a hundred tries, and an attacker gets as many tries as they like.

3. 🔱 The Fork

Option Choose when What it costs you Tell-tale signal
Break exfiltration Outputs can go to a human, not a channel. The usual first choice. No email, webhook or arbitrary-URL tools; markdown images and links need restricting too. The tool list has a "send" or "fetch URL" that the use case never needed.
Break private data The task doesn't genuinely need the sensitive corpus. Capability — the agent can't answer about what it can't read. Broad read scopes granted "just in case".
Break untrusted content Inputs are enumerable and sources allowlistable. The open web, user attachments, inbound mail. Content arriving from anywhere a stranger can put it.
Harden all three You genuinely can't remove one — then this is damage limitation, not a defence. Probabilistic; fails at scale by the arithmetic below. "We added an injection classifier" offered as the answer.

4. 📐 What It Flips

If you choose Architecture changes Budget changes Ops changes
Break exfiltration Outbound tools deleted or moved behind a human; egress allowlist on the sandbox; output rendering sanitised. Cheapest — mostly removal. A human in the loop on anything that leaves, and a review of what rendering can smuggle.
Break private data A scoped retrieval layer; the agent reads a filtered view, not the corpus. A filtering layer, and re-derived answers when scope changes. Per-request scope becomes an auditable decision.
Break untrusted content An allowlist at every ingestion point, and provenance carried with every document. Source vetting is ongoing work, not a one-off. Someone owns the allowlist, and the pressure to widen it never stops.
Harden all three A classifier and filters in the path — boxes that do not change the reachability. Ongoing tuning, false positives on real traffic. An alert stream, and a false confidence that is itself a risk.

Someone holding this table can redraw the diagram, because three of the four rows delete edges rather than adding boxes. That's the tell for a real mitigation here: if your answer adds a component and every original path still exists, you have not broken a leg.

5. 🔢 The Numbers

Why detection isn't a leg. A filter that catches a share d of injection attempts lets each one through with probability 1 − d. Over n independent attempts, the chance that none gets through is:

P(all caught) = d ⁿ

At a generous d = 0.99:

  • n = 100 → 0.99¹⁰⁰ = 0.366, so a 63% chance at least one lands
  • n = 1000 → 0.99¹⁰⁰⁰ ≈ 0.000043, i.e. one lands, effectively certainly

An attacker chooses n. A defender who has broken a leg has an outcome that doesn't depend on n at all — with no outbound channel, exfiltration is impossible regardless of how many injections succeed. That difference, between a probability that decays with attempts and a property that holds, is the whole argument for architecture over filtering.

The measured price of breaking a leg by design. CaMeL extracts control and data flow from the trusted query so retrieved content can never influence the program's path, and enforces capabilities at tool-call time. It solves 77% of AgentDojo tasks with provable security, against 84% undefended — about seven points of task success, roughly an 8% relative drop. That's the honest number to quote when someone asks what the secure design costs: it is not free, and it is also not the 50% people fear.

What the cheapest leg actually costs. Breaking exfiltration is mostly deletion, so the cost is capability you were carrying anyway. The trap is that outbound channels aren't only tools: a rendered markdown image whose URL contains data, a link the user is invited to click, an error message echoed to a third-party service — all are channels. The audit is "enumerate every way bytes can leave", and it is longer than the tool list.

Combining, rather than choosing. The legs aren't exclusive. Removing outbound tools and scoping data down multiplies the reduction, and in a design round it's worth saying which one is load-bearing — the one you'd defend if the product manager asked for the other back.

6. 🧭 The Decision Procedure

There is deliberately no branch that terminates in "add a classifier". A filter is worth having as depth once a leg is broken, and it is never the terminal answer — the last node is a human precisely because when all three legs are genuinely required, the only thing left that isn't probabilistic is a person deciding.

7. 💥 Failure Story

Symptom. "A customer's support history appeared in a request to a domain nobody recognised."

Root cause. All three legs were present and nobody had said so out loud. The agent read the customer's ticket history (private data), summarised attachments the customer had uploaded (untrusted content), and rendered its answer as markdown in an internal console (the outbound channel — nobody had counted it as one). An attachment contained instructions to include an image whose URL embedded the conversation summary. The console rendered the image, the browser fetched it, and the data left. No tool was called; no tool needed to be.

Fix. Image and link rendering were restricted to an allowlisted set of hosts, which broke the exfiltration leg without touching capability. The expensive part was retrospective: because the channel was a rendering behaviour rather than a tool call, the traces recorded a normal successful run, and establishing which conversations had been affected meant replaying rendered output rather than reading an audit log — the audit trail recorded decisions, not what the page had fetched.

8. 🎤 How It's Probed

Tier 1 — Clarification

You keep saying "break a leg". Why isn't defence in depth the answer?

Defence in depth is the right posture once a leg is broken, and it is not a substitute for breaking one. The difference is what happens as attempts accumulate: layered probabilistic filters still leave a per-attempt success probability, and an attacker with unlimited tries converges on success. Removing a leg changes the outcome from unlikely to impossible for that class.

So I'd offer both, in order. Break the cheapest leg first, then add filtering, marking of untrusted content and output validation behind it — as the thing that reduces noise and catches mistakes, not as the control the design rests on.

Tier 2 — Trade-off

Breaking exfiltration removes the agent's ability to act. Doesn't that defeat the point?

It removes the ability to act autonomously and outbound, which is narrower than it sounds. A support agent that drafts a reply for a human to send has broken the leg and still does nearly all of the work — the saving was in the drafting, not the pressing of send. Most products that claim to need an outbound channel need a proposal channel.

Where it genuinely bites is unattended automation, and there I'd rather narrow the channel than remove it. An outbound tool with a fixed recipient and a fixed template is not an exfiltration channel in any useful sense, because the attacker controls neither where it goes nor what it carries. The dangerous shape is a general-purpose send with attacker-influenceable destination and body, and that shape is usually a convenience rather than a requirement.

Tier 3 — Edge case / scaling

What breaks when this system serves a hundred tenants instead of one?

The data leg, because it is the one that is per-tenant rather than global. A single-tenant deployment can break it by scoping the corpus once; a multi-tenant one has to enforce scope on every retrieval, every cache read and every memory write, and any of those that forgets the tenant key rebuilds the leg for everyone at once.

The exfiltration leg scales better because it's a property of the tool list and the renderer, which are global. That asymmetry is an argument for choosing exfiltration as the leg you break in a multi-tenant product: it's the one where correctness doesn't have to be re-established per request.

Tier 4 — Open-ended design

Design an agent that triages inbound email and files tickets.

Inbound email is untrusted content by definition and cannot be allowlisted, and the ticket system is private data, so two legs are fixed. That means the entire design rests on the third, and I'd say so before drawing anything: no outbound mail tool, no URL fetching, and ticket creation restricted to a fixed schema with no free-text field the model controls that is ever rendered back to a user.

The subtle part is that ticket creation is itself a channel. If the agent can write arbitrary text into a ticket that a colleague's browser renders, an injected instruction can place a tracking URL there. So the write is schema-bound — enumerated fields, no markdown, no links — and that constraint comes from the trifecta rather than from any idea about data modelling.

What I'd flag as residual: the agent still summarises attacker-controlled text into a field a human reads, so the remaining risk is social rather than technical — the injected content persuading a person. That's a real risk and it's a different control, which is where the approval gate and the audit trail come in.

9. ⚠️ Traps & Misconceptions

❌ Trap: "We added a prompt-injection classifier, so we're covered."

✅ Reality: A 99% filter lets one through within a hundred attempts. The attacker picks the number of attempts. Filters are depth behind a broken leg, never the leg itself.

❌ Trap: "We have no outbound tools, so there's no exfiltration path."

✅ Reality: A rendered image URL, a clickable link, an error forwarded to a third party — all carry bytes out. The audit is "how can data leave", which is longer than the tool list.

❌ Trap: "Secure agent designs don't work well enough to ship."

✅ Reality: CaMeL solves 77% of AgentDojo tasks with provable security against 84% undefended. Seven points is a real price and a very different conversation from "it doesn't work".

10. 🔗 Connections

⬆️ Depends on (concepts assumed)

  • The lethal trifecta — the framing this note resolves.

  • prompt injection in agents — the attack this defends against.

🔁 Decides / constrains (other decisions this one forces)

  • §11 Whose authority the tool call runs with — scoping data down is enforced by whose credentials the call uses.

  • §11 Which boundary untrusted code runs behind — egress control is how the exfiltration leg stays broken.

  • §11 Where the approval gate sits — the human in the last branch of the procedure.

  • §4 Read tools vs write tools — the outbound tools this note deletes are the same ones that fork classifies.

🏗️ Design problems that hinge on this

  • §14 Email triage agent — two legs are fixed by the brief, so the third is the whole design.

  • §14 Deep research agent — reads the open web, so the content leg is unavailable and the other two carry it.

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • Audience binding and the normative ban on token passthrough — MCP specification: authorization

  • The risk class this fork exists to close — OWASP LLM06:2025 Excessive Agency

  • Capabilities enforced at tool-call time rather than trusted in the prompt — Defeating prompt injections by design — CaMeL (arXiv 2503.18813)

0. 🔒 Owned Elsewhere

Concepts assumed (don't re-read unless rusty):

  • permissions and least privilege — the principle and the five scoping axes.

  • excessive agency — what too much authority produces.

What this note adds: the sourcing decision. "Least privilege" says how narrow; this says whose credential the call runs with, which is what actually decides whether a confused deputy is possible — and the blast-radius arithmetic that ranks the four answers.

1. 🎯 Recall Check

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
Confused deputy, in one line? The agent's authority exceeds the requester's, and it acts anyway.
Blast radius, as a product? Resources reachable × permissions held × time the credential lives.
Why token passthrough is banned? A token not issued for that server lets it act as a deputy elsewhere.
Cheapest real improvement? Per-tool credentials instead of one agent identity.
What JIT minting costs? A minting service on the hot path, and more to operate.

2. The Decision in 30 Seconds

The default that gets shipped is one service account the agent holds for everything, and it's the wrong one, because the agent then has authority no individual requester has — that's the confused deputy, and prompt injection is simply the cheapest way to exploit it. My default is delegated user credentials wherever a user is identifiable, so the agent can never exceed the person who asked, and per-tool scoped credentials for the machine-to-machine parts. I go to just-in-time minted capabilities for the high-value writes, where a credential that lives seconds and names one resource is worth the minting service it costs. The pivot is whether a human identity exists at all: unattended automation has no user to delegate from, and then narrowing scope per tool is the only lever left.

3. 🔱 The Fork

Option Choose when What it costs you Tell-tale signal
One agent service account Prototypes only. Blast radius is everything it can reach, indefinitely; the audit log says "the agent did it". One API key in the environment, used by every request.
Per-tool scoped credentials Unattended automation with no user identity. A credential per tool to provision and rotate. One token satisfying tools that need nothing in common.
Delegated user credentials A named user is on the request. The default. A consent flow, per-user token storage and refresh — and the agent inherits an over-broad user. The agent can do things the requesting user cannot.
JIT-minted capability per call High-value or irreversible writes. A minting service in the hot path; more to run and to debug. A standing credential with scopes exercised once a month.

4. 📐 What It Flips

If you choose Architecture changes Budget changes Ops changes
Agent service account Nothing — which is why it happens. None. Every incident is org-wide; attribution is impossible.
Per-tool credentials A credential store keyed by tool; the tool layer resolves it. Provisioning and rotation work per tool. Blast radius is one tool's scope; revocation is surgical.
Delegated user An OAuth flow, token storage, refresh, and an identity threaded through every call. Latency on first use; storage per user. Audit reads "user X, via agent"; revoking the user revokes the agent.
JIT capability A minting service; tools accept a capability rather than a credential. A synchronous hop per privileged call. Leaked credentials expire before they're useful; issuance itself becomes the audit.

The redraw test lands hard here: the first row draws no box, and the other three each add one — a credential store, an authorization server, or a minting service. Any answer to "how do you do least privilege" that adds no box has not changed who the call runs as.

5. 🔢 The Numbers

Blast radius as a product. What a compromised or injected agent can do is bounded by three factors:

blast radius ≈ resources reachable × permissions held × credential lifetime

The four options differ by orders of magnitude on each. A service account with org-wide read and write reaches every resource, holds every permission, and lives until someone rotates it — unbounded on all three. A delegated user token reaches that user's resources for the token's lifetime, typically an hour. A JIT capability names one resource, one operation, and lives seconds. That's the whole argument, and it's multiplicative rather than additive — narrowing any one factor helps, narrowing all three is what makes the difference categorical.

Why the audit consequence matters as much as the security one. With a shared service account every action is attributed to the agent, so "who authorised this" has no answer and revocation is all-or-nothing. With delegated credentials the log names a person, and revoking that person revokes their agent without affecting anyone else. That operational property usually sells the design faster than the security argument.

The confused deputy, stated precisely. The agent holds authority A. A requester holds authority R. If the agent acts on the requester's instruction using A, then the requester has effectively been granted A, and the interesting part is A \ R — everything the agent can do that the requester cannot. Prompt injection is one way to reach A \ R; a curious employee asking politely is another, and it doesn't require an attacker at all. The fix is not to detect the instruction, it is to make A ⊆ R by construction.

What the protocols already mandate. The MCP authorization spec requires that servers validate tokens were issued specifically for them as the intended audience, that clients must not send tokens other than ones issued by that server's authorization server, and that servers must not accept or transit any other tokens. Token passthrough — forwarding a token you were given to a downstream service — is exactly the deputy pattern, and it is a normative MUST NOT rather than a recommendation. The same spec defines a step-up flow where an insufficient scope returns 403 with the scopes needed, which is what makes narrow-by-default practical instead of merely virtuous.

6. 🧭 The Decision Procedure

The first question is the only one that matters structurally, because delegation is the single change that makes A ⊆ R hold by construction rather than by policy. Everything below it narrows a radius that delegation has already bounded — worth doing, and second-order by comparison.

7. 💥 Failure Story

Symptom. "A contractor used the assistant to pull a salary report they had no access to."

Root cause. The agent authenticated to the internal data platform with its own service account, provisioned broadly during the pilot so that every team's questions would work without a permissions project. Authorisation was enforced in the system prompt — an instruction describing which roles could ask about which datasets — and the model followed it most of the time. The contractor did not need an injection or a jailbreak; they asked a question phrased as a normal reporting request, and the model complied. Every layer behaved as built: the platform saw a legitimate, fully-authorised query from a trusted service account.

Fix. The agent moved to delegated credentials, obtaining a token for the requesting user and querying as them, so the platform's existing row-level rules applied unchanged and the prompt stopped being a security control. Applying it late was the expensive part: the pilot's convenience had become an assumption in four downstream features that queried across tenants, and each needed a legitimate service path before the broad account could be revoked.

8. 🎤 How It's Probed

Tier 1 — Clarification

If the prompt says the agent may only read HR data for HR users, why isn't that enough?

Because the prompt is an instruction to a probabilistic system, and the resource it protects doesn't consult it. The data platform sees a valid credential with the right scope and serves the query; nothing in the enforcement path ever reads the policy. So the control's reliability is the model's instruction-following rate, on adversarial and non-adversarial inputs alike.

The general rule is that a control has to live where the decision is enforced. If the model decides, the model is the control — and a component you can talk out of an answer is not one you want holding authority. Moving it to the credential means the check happens in a system with no natural language in it.

Tier 2 — Trade-off

Delegated credentials sound right, but the agent then inherits an over-privileged user. Isn't that the same problem?

It's a smaller problem with a different owner, which is real progress. The agent can no longer exceed the requester, so A \ R is empty and the confused deputy is gone; what remains is that R is too large. That's an ordinary access-review problem, it has an owner, and fixing it helps every system that user touches.

Where I'd go further is on writes. Reads inherit the user's scope quite safely, but an irreversible write is worth narrowing beyond it — a minted capability naming the one resource and expiring in seconds, so that even a fully-authorised user's session can't be replayed into a second, unintended write. That's the point where the minting service pays for itself.

Tier 3 — Edge case / scaling

What breaks with delegated credentials when runs are long or asynchronous?

Token lifetime stops matching run lifetime. A run that pauses for a human approval overnight holds a token that expired hours ago, and the naive fixes are both wrong: storing a refresh token so the agent can act indefinitely without the user present recreates a standing credential, and extending lifetimes widens the window on every leak.

The shape that works makes the pause a boundary: the run checkpoints, releases its credential, and re-acquires authority on resume — from a still-valid session or by asking again. That's the durable-pause machinery §7 needs anyway, and a resumable run and a re-authorised run turn out to be the same mechanism.

Tier 4 — Open-ended design

Design authority for an agent platform where tenants install third-party tools.

Two trust domains that must not share a credential. Platform tools run with per-tool scoped credentials the platform provisions; third-party tools never receive a platform credential, and never a token minted for anything but themselves — the audience-binding rule, which is the whole defence against an installed tool using its position to act elsewhere.

For user data, delegation per tenant per tool: the user consents to that specific tool's scopes, and the resulting token names that tool as its audience. The consent screen is the security boundary as much as the token is, so it has to name the tool and the scopes rather than the platform, or users are approving something they can't evaluate.

The part I'd raise unprompted is revocation. Installed tools accumulate and nobody uninstalls them, so I'd want expiry by default rather than revocation on demand — tokens that die unless re-consented beat a list nobody prunes. Designing for what's still installed in two years is more of the posture than the first grant is.

9. ⚠️ Traps & Misconceptions

❌ Trap: "We apply least privilege — the agent's account only has the scopes it needs."

✅ Reality: The agent's needs are the union of every user's needs, so its account is broader than any individual's. That union is precisely the confused deputy. Narrow scopes on a shared identity doesn't fix whose identity it is.

❌ Trap: "We pass the user's token through to the downstream service."

✅ Reality: A token issued for one audience being replayed at another is the deputy pattern in protocol form — a normative MUST NOT in the MCP spec. Exchange it for one minted for that audience.

❌ Trap: "Authorisation rules in the system prompt keep the agent in its lane."

✅ Reality: The resource never reads the prompt. A control that only exists in natural language is enforced by instruction-following, which is neither auditable nor adversarially reliable.

10. 🔗 Connections

⬆️ Depends on (concepts assumed)

  • permissions and least privilege — the scoping axes this note sources credentials for.

  • excessive agency — the failure this bounds.

🔁 Decides / constrains (other decisions this one forces)

  • §11 Which leg of the trifecta you break — scoping private data down is enforced here or not at all.

  • §11 Isolation by filter or by construction — per-tenant credentials are the strongest form of that isolation.

  • §4 Adopt MCP, and build a server or consume one — audience binding is a protocol obligation of that choice.

  • §7 How a run waits for a human without holding anything — a paused run must not hold a live credential.

🏗️ Design problems that hinge on this

  • §14 Enterprise assistant over internal data — delegation is the difference between a demo and something legal will approve.

  • §14 Multi-tenant agent platform — third-party tools make audience binding load-bearing.

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • The microVM numbers that decide whether per-run isolation is affordable — Firecracker

  • Kernel-surface isolation without hardware virtualisation — gVisor documentation

  • The risk class an unbounded action space falls under — OWASP LLM06:2025 Excessive Agency

0. 🔒 Owned Elsewhere

Concepts assumed (don't re-read unless rusty):

  • sandboxing and isolation — containers, microVMs and what each isolates.

  • the expanded attack surface — why code execution widens it.

What this note adds: that this is two decisions, not one. A sandbox bounds what code can touch on the host; egress policy bounds what it can send off it. Teams pick a boundary, call it sandboxed, and leave the second axis at default-allow — and the arithmetic of per-run isolation, which is cheaper than most people assume.

1. 🎯 Recall Check

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
The two axes? Isolation boundary (host) and egress policy (network).
What a container doesn't isolate? The kernel — a shared surface, so an escape reaches the host.
Cost of a fresh microVM per run? Under 125ms boot, under 5 MiB overhead.
What sandboxing does for exfiltration? Nothing, unless egress is denied by default.
Why reuse a sandbox across runs? Speed — at the price of cross-run contamination.

2. The Decision in 30 Seconds

I treat the boundary and the network as separate decisions, because a sandbox that can still reach the internet has protected the host and not the data. For the boundary my default is a fresh microVM or gVisor-class sandbox per run rather than a container, since the container shares the host kernel and that's the surface an escape uses — and per-run isolation is affordable: a microVM boots in under 125 milliseconds with under 5 MiB of overhead, which is noise inside a multi-second agent run. Egress is default-deny with an allowlist, always. The pivot is reuse: if a sandbox is reused between runs to save the boot, you've traded isolation between tenants for milliseconds you didn't need.

3. 🔱 The Fork

Option Choose when What it costs you Tell-tale signal
No sandbox — in-process Never, once code is model-generated. Everything the host process can reach. exec or eval called on model output.
Container Trusted code, untrusted input. A shared kernel — an escape lands on the host with your other workloads. "It's in Docker, so it's isolated."
microVM or gVisor Model-generated code. The default. Boot latency per run; an extra runtime to operate. Arbitrary code, arbitrary packages, arbitrary intent.
Remote managed sandbox You'd rather buy the isolation than run it. A network hop per call, and data leaving your perimeter to be executed. No appetite to operate a hypervisor fleet.

4. 📐 What It Flips

If you choose Architecture changes Budget changes Ops changes
Container A runtime boundary and an image to maintain. Cheapest; milliseconds to start. Kernel CVEs become your agent's CVEs.
microVM / gVisor A pool or a per-run launcher; a filesystem contract for getting work in and results out. Under 125ms per run; up to ~150 microVMs per second per host. A second runtime to patch — and blast radius stops at the VM.
Remote managed An API call replacing local execution. Per-second or per-call billing instead of capacity. Someone else's availability; a data-residency conversation.
Egress default-deny An allowlisting proxy, and a list someone owns. Negligible. Every new dependency becomes a request to widen the list — which is the control working.

The egress row is the one that changes reachability rather than boxes, which is why it gets skipped: the diagram looks identical before and after. It is also the only row on this table that addresses data leaving, and the other three do not touch it at all.

5. 🔢 The Numbers

Per-run isolation is cheaper than the instinct says. A microVM boots in under 125ms with under 5 MiB of memory overhead, and a host can create up to 150 per second. Against an agent run that takes seconds to tens of seconds, a fresh VM per run is on the order of 1–3% of wall-clock:

overhead share = 0.125s / run duration

At a 5-second run that's 2.5%; at a 30-second run, 0.4%. Reuse buys back a fraction of a percent and costs you the property that one run cannot observe another's leftovers — which is a bad trade at almost any run length, and an obviously bad one in a multi-tenant system.

Density, for the capacity question that follows. At under 5 MiB of overhead, isolation is not what limits concurrency — the workload's own memory is. That matters because "we can't afford a VM per run" is usually an assumption rather than a measurement, and the measurement disagrees.

Why the boundary choice is about the kernel, not the process. Containers isolate namespaces and cgroups on a shared kernel, so the attack surface is the whole syscall interface: a kernel vulnerability reaches the host and everything else on it. gVisor interposes a user-space kernel so that surface shrinks to what it re-implements; a microVM replaces it with a hardware virtualisation boundary. The practical question in a round is "what does an escape reach", and for a container the honest answer is your other workloads.

The egress axis, stated as arithmetic. Isolation reduces what code can touch to the sandbox. It does not reduce what code can send, because outbound network is a normal capability of a sandboxed process. With default-allow egress, the exfiltration probability given code execution is essentially 1 — a single HTTP request suffices. With default-deny and an allowlist, it's 0 for any destination not on the list, regardless of what the code tried. Same binary-versus-probabilistic distinction as breaking a trifecta leg, and it's the same reason it's worth doing.

6. 🧭 The Decision Procedure

Every path terminates on the egress decision deliberately. The boundary question has three defensible answers depending on what you're willing to run, and the egress question has one — which is why drawing it as the terminal node is more honest than listing it as a consideration.

7. 💥 Failure Story

Symptom. "Customer data from the analysis sandbox turned up in a paste site."

Root cause. Code execution had been reviewed carefully and the boundary was genuinely good: a fresh container per run, no host mounts, a read-only root filesystem, dropped capabilities. The review had asked "what can this code reach on our machines" and answered it well. Nobody asked what it could reach on the internet, and the container had ordinary outbound network because every base image does. An injected instruction in an uploaded spreadsheet produced code that read the data it had legitimately been given and posted it outward in a single request. The sandbox worked exactly as designed and was irrelevant to the incident.

Fix. Egress moved to default-deny through an allowlisting proxy, with the package index and two internal endpoints on the list. The late cost was that several legitimate workflows had been quietly depending on open network — a chart library fetching fonts, a job pulling a dataset by URL — so the allowlist had to be discovered from traffic rather than designed, and every one of those discoveries was a path that had been available to an attacker for as long as the feature had existed.

8. 🎤 How It's Probed

Tier 1 — Clarification

Docker is isolation. Why isn't a container enough for model-generated code?

Because the isolation is namespaces and cgroups over a kernel the host shares. The container restricts what the process sees, not what it can ask the kernel to do, so the reachable attack surface is the full syscall interface — and a kernel bug there puts the attacker on the host beside whatever else you run.

For trusted code handling untrusted input that's usually an acceptable trade, since the code isn't trying to escape. For code the model wrote from an attacker-influenceable prompt, the code itself is the untrusted thing, and the appropriate boundary is one that doesn't share a kernel — a microVM, or a user-space kernel like gVisor that shrinks the surface to what it re-implements.

Tier 2 — Trade-off

Fresh sandbox per run versus a warm pool — how do you decide?

I start from fresh-per-run and make the pool justify itself, because the arithmetic rarely supports it. A microVM boots in under 125ms, so on a five-second run the pool buys back about two percent of wall-clock, and what it costs is the guarantee that one run leaves nothing for the next.

The place pooling genuinely earns its keep is interactive, single-tenant work where the state is the product — a notebook-style session where the user expects variables to persist across turns. There the sandbox lifetime is the session rather than the run, which is a different and defensible boundary. What I'd refuse is pooling across tenants to save the boot, because that turns a latency optimisation into a data-isolation decision without anyone recording it as one.

Tier 3 — Edge case / scaling

What breaks at a thousand concurrent sandboxed runs?

Not memory — at under 5 MiB of overhead, isolation isn't the constraint, the workloads are. Creation rate can be, at up to ~150 microVMs per second per host, so a spike of a thousand simultaneous starts serialises across a handful of seconds unless you spread it over hosts or keep a small warm buffer.

The thing that actually breaks first is usually the egress allowlist, because at scale it becomes a shared bottleneck and a shared blast radius. One proxy for every tenant's sandbox means one misconfiguration exposes all of them, and a widened entry granted for one customer's workflow is granted to everyone's. Per-tenant egress policy is the scaling answer, and it's more work than the sandbox.

Tier 4 — Open-ended design

Design execution for a data-analysis agent over customer uploads.

The upload is untrusted content and the generated code is untrusted code, so both legs are attacker-influenceable and this is the shape that most needs a real boundary. Fresh microVM per run, no reuse, the customer's file mounted read-only, results returned through a structured channel rather than a shared filesystem.

Egress default-deny with nothing on the allowlist, which is unusually achievable here: an analysis workload needs no network at all if its dependencies are baked into the image. That turns the exfiltration probability to zero rather than small, and it removes the pressure to widen a list later, because there is no list.

The remaining channel is the result itself — the agent summarises attacker-influenceable data into text a human reads, so a URL can still be smuggled out through the rendered answer. That's the same rendering channel that breaks the trifecta's third leg, and it's worth saying out loud that sandboxing did not address it, because the natural assumption in the room is that it did.

9. ⚠️ Traps & Misconceptions

❌ Trap: "The code runs in a sandbox, so we're safe."

✅ Reality: A sandbox bounds what code touches on the host. Outbound network is a normal capability of a sandboxed process, so with default-allow egress, exfiltration given execution is near-certain.

❌ Trap: "A VM per run is too expensive."

✅ Reality: Under 125ms and under 5 MiB. On a five-second run that's 2.5% of wall-clock. The cost objection is usually an assumption that hasn't been measured.

❌ Trap: "We reuse warm sandboxes for speed."

✅ Reality: Fine within one user's session, and a data-isolation decision across tenants. Saving 125ms by letting one tenant's run inherit another's filesystem is a trade nobody would approve if it were written down that way.

10. 🔗 Connections

⬆️ Depends on (concepts assumed)

  • sandboxing and isolation — the boundaries this note prices.

  • the expanded attack surface — why code execution is the widest surface.

🔁 Decides / constrains (other decisions this one forces)

  • §11 Which leg of the trifecta you break — egress default-deny is how the exfiltration leg stays broken.

  • §11 Isolation by filter or by construction — sandbox reuse across tenants is that decision in disguise.

  • §4 Give the agent a shell, or keep the action space typed — this note prices the shell option.

  • §9 Which term in the latency sum you attack — sandbox boot is a real term in a code-executing agent.

🏗️ Design problems that hinge on this

  • §14 Data-analysis agent over uploads — untrusted code and untrusted data at once.

  • §14 Coding agent — the sandbox is the product boundary, and egress is what stops a repo leaving.

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • The risk class an ungated action path falls under — OWASP LLM06:2025 Excessive Agency

  • Enforcing a policy at tool-call time instead of trusting the loop — Defeating prompt injections by design — CaMeL (arXiv 2503.18813)

  • Patterns that make a path's safety a property rather than a hope — Design patterns for securing LLM agents against prompt injections (arXiv 2506.08837)

0. 🔒 Owned Elsewhere

Concepts assumed (don't re-read unless rusty):

  • human-in-the-loop — what an approval step is and when to ask for one.

  • excessive agency — the harm an ungated action causes.

What this note adds: the audit. A gate is easy; proving no path reaches the effect without crossing it is the actual work, because tools compose — two individually harmless calls can produce an irreversible effect that neither one is gated for.

1. 🎯 Recall Check

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
Where the gate belongs? The tool layer — the chokepoint every path crosses.
What the audit asks? Is there a path from untrusted input to an effect crossing no gate?
Why a tool list isn't enough? Effects compose; two ungated reads can add up to a write.
What frequent gates cost? Habituation — a gate that fires often is rubber-stamped.
The gate's own attack surface? The summary shown to the approver, which the attacker may control.

2. The Decision in 30 Seconds

The gate goes in the tool layer, because that's the one chokepoint every path crosses regardless of what the model decided — in the loop it can be reasoned around, and in the prompt it isn't a control at all. But placing it is the easy half. The half that's actually graded is the audit: I'd enumerate every externally-visible effect, then check whether any path from an untrusted input reaches one without crossing a gate, including paths that compose two tools that are individually innocuous. And the pivot is frequency — a gate that fires on most runs gets rubber-stamped, so a gate you approve without reading is worse than no gate, because it has an audit trail that says a human agreed.

3. 🔱 The Fork

Option Choose when What it costs you Tell-tale signal
In the prompt Never — it isn't an enforcement point. Nothing, and it enforces nothing. "Always ask the user before sending" in a system prompt.
In the agent loop Single harness, low stakes, speed matters. Bypassed by any path that doesn't run the loop — retries, replays, a second entry point. The gate is an if statement in the orchestration code.
In the tool layer Anything irreversible. The default. A gate every caller crosses, including your own batch jobs. Several entry points reach the same effectful tool.
At the resource Regulated or highest value. Slowest to change; the resource owner now owns your UX. The downstream system already has an approval workflow.

4. 📐 What It Flips

If you choose Architecture changes Budget changes Ops changes
Loop gate A branch in the orchestrator. Free. Every new entry point silently skips it.
Tool-layer gate A policy check in front of tool dispatch; a pause/resume path for the run. A durable pause, which the run must survive. One place to audit and one place to change a policy.
Resource gate None of yours — theirs. Their latency becomes yours. Enforcement you can point to in an audit, and can't tune.
Add the reachability audit Nothing at runtime; a model of the tool graph in CI. A test that fails a build when a new tool opens a path. Adding an effectful tool becomes a reviewed event.

The last row adds no runtime box, which is why it never gets built — and it's the one that turns "we have approval gates" into something you can demonstrate. A gate you placed is a claim; a failing test on an ungated path is evidence.

5. 🔢 The Numbers

The audit is a reachability question, not a checklist. Model tools as edges. Let U be the set of nodes where untrusted content enters — retrieval, inbound mail, uploads, tool results from third parties — and E the set of externally-visible effects: sends, writes, payments, deletions, posts. The property you want is:

for every u ∈ U and every e ∈ E:
    every path u → e crosses a gate

This is ordinary graph reachability over the tool graph, and it can be a CI test rather than a review opinion. The value is that it fails when someone adds a tool, which is when gate coverage actually regresses — nobody removes a gate, they add an edge that goes around one.

Why the tool list understates it. Coverage is not "gated effectful tools ÷ effectful tools", because effects compose. create_draft and schedule_send are each defensible as ungated; together they are an ungated send. fetch_url plus write_file is a download. Paths grow combinatorially while the list grows linearly — which is why the review that walks the tool list always passes and the incident happens anyway.

Gate frequency and habituation. A gate's real catch rate isn't its coverage, it's coverage times the probability a human actually reads it. If a gate fires on a large share of runs, approvals become a reflex, and the effective rate collapses toward zero while the audit log still records deliberate human consent — worse than no gate, because it manufactures evidence of a decision nobody made. The design consequence: make gates rare by narrowing what trips them, rather than safe by making them frequent. A gate that fires on 2% of runs and is read is worth more than one that fires on half and isn't.

The gate's own attack surface. The approver decides from a summary, and if attacker-influenceable content can shape that summary, the gate has been routed around without being bypassed. So the approval surface shows the structured effect — recipient, amount, resource id, operation — from the validated tool arguments, never a model-authored description of what it is about to do. That distinction is small in the diagram and is the difference between a control and a formality.

6. 🧭 The Decision Procedure

The reversibility question comes first because it's the one that keeps the gate count low, and a low gate count is what keeps approvals meaningful. Everything that can be undone inside the run gets logged rather than gated, which reserves the human's attention for the things that genuinely can't.

7. 💥 Failure Story

Symptom. "Two hundred customers got an email the agent was never supposed to be able to send."

Root cause. Sending was gated — the send_email tool required approval, and it had never been approved without a human reading it. What wasn't gated was create_draft, reasonably classified as reversible, and a scheduled-delivery feature added months later by a different team, which published drafts marked ready. Neither tool sent anything on its own. Composed, they were an ungated send, and an injected instruction in a customer's inbound message walked the agent along that path. The review that signed off the scheduler asked whether it had an external effect and concluded correctly that it only published existing drafts.

Fix. The gate moved from send_email to the effect — anything that causes a message to leave, whoever triggers it — and the tool graph was modelled so CI could assert no path from an untrusted source reached an outbound effect ungated. Applying it late cost a full audit of every tool added in the intervening year, because the question "which of these compose into an effect" had never been asked and the answer wasn't in any document.

8. 🎤 How It's Probed

Tier 1 — Clarification

The loop already checks before calling a write tool. Why move the gate to the tool layer?

Because the loop is one caller among several, and the others appear later — a retry path, a replayed run, a batch job, a second agent, a test endpoint. Each reaches the tool without passing the orchestrator's branch. The gate belongs where the effect is unavoidable, and that's dispatch.

It also changes what you can say about the system. A gate in the loop supports "our agent asks first"; a gate at dispatch supports "this effect cannot occur without an approval record". The second is a property, the first is a behaviour, and only one of them survives a new entry point being added by someone who never read the design doc.

Tier 2 — Trade-off

Gating everything irreversible sounds safe but unusable. Where's the line?

Reversible-within-the-run is the line I'd defend, and it does more work than it looks. A draft you can delete, a record you can revert, a file in a scratch space — all logged, none gated. What gets gated is what leaves your control: a message delivered, money moved, a third party notified, data deleted past a recovery window.

The reason to keep the set small is habituation, not usability. A gate firing constantly isn't annoying, it's broken — approved without reading, while the log records deliberate consent. So when the set grows my instinct is to reduce what's irreversible, with an undo window or a staging step, rather than to gate more. That converts a security problem into a product one, which is usually where it's cheaper.

Tier 3 — Edge case / scaling

What breaks when the tool catalogue grows from ten tools to two hundred?

The audit, first, because the paths grow combinatorially while the list grows linearly. At ten tools a careful person can hold the composition in their head; at two hundred nobody can, and the review reverts to checking each tool in isolation — which is the check that passes right before the incident. That's the argument for making it a CI test while the graph is still small enough to model by hand.

Second is the classification. At scale, tools arrive from teams that don't share your threat model, and "does this have an external effect" gets answered optimistically by whoever wants to ship. So the classification is declared in the tool definition and reviewed like a schema change, not inferred by whoever runs the audit.

Tier 4 — Open-ended design

Design approvals for an agent that takes actions on a customer's account.

I'd gate on the effect, at dispatch, with the trigger derived from reversibility and value rather than from tool names — so a refund under a threshold is logged and one above it is approved, and the threshold is configuration rather than code. The approval surface shows the structured arguments the tool will actually receive: account, amount, operation. Not the model's description of them.

The run then needs to survive the wait, which is why this decision drags in durable pause. A gate that holds a process open is a gate that expires when a deployment rolls, so the run checkpoints, releases its credential, and resumes on approval — the same machinery §7 builds for other reasons.

The part I'd raise unprompted is denial. Most designs specify the happy path and leave rejection as an exception, so the agent retries, rephrases and asks again — turning a denied action into a repeated request until someone approves. Denial has to be terminal for that plan, recorded, and fed back as a fact the agent cannot argue with, or the gate becomes a negotiation.

9. ⚠️ Traps & Misconceptions

❌ Trap: "Every write tool requires approval, so irreversible actions are covered."

✅ Reality: Effects compose. A draft plus a scheduler is a send; a fetch plus a write is a download. The audit is over paths through the tool graph, and the tool list always passes.

❌ Trap: "More gates means more safety."

✅ Reality: A gate that fires constantly is rubber-stamped, and it produces an audit trail claiming a human agreed. Rare and read beats frequent and reflexive.

❌ Trap: "We show the user what the agent plans to do before it does it."

✅ Reality: If that summary is model-authored from attacker-influenceable content, the attacker writes the approval screen. Show the validated structured arguments, not a description of them.

10. 🔗 Connections

⬆️ Depends on (concepts assumed)

  • human-in-the-loop — the approval step this note places and audits.

  • excessive agency — the harm an ungated path produces.

🔁 Decides / constrains (other decisions this one forces)

  • §11 Which leg of the trifecta you break — the human in that procedure's last branch is this gate.

  • §11 Whether the audit trail is logging or a record of decision — the approval record is the part that must be evidence.

  • §2 Where authority to act lives — the tool layer holds the gate for the same reason it holds authority.

  • §7 How a run waits for a human without holding anything — a gate is only as durable as the pause behind it.

🏗️ Design problems that hinge on this

  • §14 Support agent that takes actions — refunds and account changes are the gated set.

  • §14 Email triage agent — the composition failure above is native to that design.

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • The risk classes rails are usually bought to cover — OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025

  • Enforcing policy at the tool call rather than in the model's reasoning — Defeating prompt injections by design — CaMeL (arXiv 2503.18813)

0. 🔒 Owned Elsewhere

Concepts assumed (don't re-read unless rusty):

  • guardrails — input, output and action rails and how each works.

  • Guardrail models & classifiers — classifier-based rails.

What this note adds: the placement rule. Rails split into two kinds with different reliability — a model judging content, and code checking a fact — and the second belongs outside the model where an injection can't reach it. Which rail you can express in code is the decision.

1. 🎯 Recall Check

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
The reliability split? Model rails are probabilistic; code rails are decidable.
Which rail matters most? The action rail — it's the one with an irreversible effect behind it.
Why policy leaves the prompt? Anything in context is subject to the injection you're defending against.

2. The Decision in 30 Seconds

I split rails by whether the check is decidable. Does this output parse, does the cited id exist, is this recipient on the allowlist, is the amount under the threshold — all code, all deterministic, and none of them can be talked out of an answer. Is this content abusive, is this request a jailbreak — those need a model, and a model rail is a probability, so it belongs as depth rather than as the control anything rests on. My default is action rails in code at the tool boundary first, output validation second, and input classification last, which is the reverse of the order teams usually build them in.

3. 🔱 The Fork

Option Choose when What it costs you Tell-tale signal
Input rails (classifier) High-volume abuse you want to shed early. Latency and cost per request; false positives on real users; misses what it hasn't seen. An abuse problem rather than a correctness one.
Output rails (schema + facts) Always — the output is structured or checkable. Nothing much; a schema you must maintain. The model returns free text where a shape was expected.
Action rails (policy in code) Any tool with an external effect. The default. A policy engine to own, and arguments that must be validated before use. A tool's arguments come straight from model output.
Policy in the prompt Never — not an enforcement point. Nothing, and it enforces nothing. Rules about what's permitted written as system-prompt prose.

4. 📐 What It Flips

If you choose Architecture changes Budget changes Ops changes
Input rail A classifier ahead of the model. A call per request, and its latency. A threshold to tune, and false positives that reach support.
Output rail Constrained decoding or a validator after generation. Occasional retries on invalid output. Schema violations become a monitorable signal rather than a mystery.
Action rail A policy engine at the tool boundary, deciding from validated arguments. Negligible per call. Policy becomes versioned, testable and reviewable outside the prompt.
Prompt policy None. None. The illusion of a control, which stops the real one being built.

The action rail is the only row where the check runs on data the attacker cannot re-word: a recipient, an amount, a resource id, already parsed. Everything upstream is judging text, which is the medium the attack is written in.

Why an input rail can't be the control. A classifier catching a share d of attempts lets each through with probability 1 − d, so over n attempts the chance none lands is dⁿ — at d = 0.99, a hundred attempts gives a 63% chance one gets through. The attacker chooses n. That is not an argument against having one; it's an argument against it being the thing you'd point at when asked how the system is safe.

7. 💥 Failure Story

Symptom. "The jailbreak classifier was at 98% in eval and the agent still leaked its instructions in week one."

Root cause. The rail was trained and measured on a static corpus of known jailbreaks, so its 98% described the past. Users iterated live, and the ones who got through published what worked, which meant the distribution the rail faced moved daily while the rail did not. More importantly the classifier was the only control: the system prompt contained the policy, so a single miss exposed everything the policy was protecting.

Fix. Policy moved out of the prompt and into the tool boundary, where the rules became code — which tools this user may call, which arguments are in range — so a successful jailbreak stopped granting anything. The classifier stayed, rescoped from a control to a signal feeding rate-limiting and review. Applying it late cost a rewrite of the tool layer, because the arguments had been passed through unvalidated on the assumption that the model had already been checked.

10. 🔗 Connections

⬆️ Depends on (concepts assumed)

  • guardrails — the three rail types this note orders.

  • Defense in depth — where a probabilistic layer legitimately sits.

🔁 Decides / constrains (other decisions this one forces)

  • §11 Where the approval gate sits — the action rail and the gate share a chokepoint.

  • §11 Which leg of the trifecta you break — rails are depth behind a broken leg, never instead of one.

  • §4 Constrain the output, or validate it after the fact — the output rail, decided there.

🏗️ Design problems that hinge on this

  • §14 Support agent that takes actions — the action rail is what makes a refund tool safe to expose.

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • A standard shape for agent, tool and model spans rather than a bespoke one — OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions

  • The disclosure risk a verbose trail creates — OWASP LLM02:2025 Sensitive Information Disclosure

0. 🔒 Owned Elsewhere

Concepts assumed (don't re-read unless rusty):

  • auditability and traceability — what to capture and why.

What this note adds: the split. Traces and audit records look like the same data and have opposite requirements — one is sampled, mutable and short-lived, the other must be complete, immutable and survive the service that wrote it. Building one thing for both jobs fails the job that matters.

1. 🎯 Recall Check

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
Why a trace isn't an audit record? Traces are sampled, mutable and expire; evidence can't be.
What must be written synchronously? Anything preceding an irreversible effect — before, not after.
The retention tension? Compliance wants years; the payload contains personal data.

2. The Decision in 30 Seconds

I build two things that look like one. Traces are for debugging — sampled, verbose, short retention, every prompt and tool result attached — and they follow a standard span convention so the tooling is off the shelf. The audit record is different: it's the set of facts that must be defensible later, written on the write path before the effect happens, append-only, and outliving the service that produced it. The reason to separate them is that the moment you need the audit trail is exactly when sampling, retention expiry or a crashed exporter will have removed it, because those are properties the debugging system was designed to have.

3. 🔱 The Fork

Option Choose when What it costs you Tell-tale signal
Traces only Internal tooling, no irreversible effects. Sampled and expiring — no answer when someone asks who approved what. "Check the logs" is the compliance answer.
Audit record only Regulated, low volume. No debugging story; reproducing a bad run is guesswork. You can prove what happened and not why.
Both, separated Anything with effects and users. The default. Two sinks, two retention policies, two schemas. Effects a customer could dispute.
One store, "just keep everything" Never, at volume. Cost, and personal data retained far past its purpose. Full prompts retained for years because deleting felt risky.

4. 📐 What It Flips

If you choose Architecture changes Budget changes Ops changes
Traces only An exporter and a backend. Cheap; sampled. Gaps are normal and acceptable — until they aren't.
Both, separated An append-only sink on the write path, alongside the trace exporter. A synchronous write before each effect. Two retention clocks, and a deletion story for each.
One store Simplest to draw. Grows without bound. A subject-access or deletion request has to reach into the evidence.

What belongs in the record, as distinct from the trace: who the requester was, whose authority the call ran with, the tool, its validated arguments, the policy decision, the approver if there was one, and the outcome. Not the prompt, and not the raw tool result — those are the trace's job, and they are where the personal data concentrates.

Write it before the effect. An audit entry written after a successful call is missing exactly the cases you need: the call that timed out having already mutated state, the process that died mid-write. Record the intent and the decision first, the outcome second — which is the same ordering the outbox pattern uses, for the same reason.

The retention tension, stated plainly. Compliance wants the record for years; data protection wants the payload gone. Separating the two sinks resolves it: the record keeps identifiers, decisions and approvers, which are small and defensible to retain, while the trace holds the content under a short clock. One combined store makes every retention question unanswerable, because deleting the personal data destroys the evidence.

7. 💥 Failure Story

Symptom. "A customer disputed an action the agent took and we couldn't show who approved it."

Root cause. Approvals were captured as trace spans, and the tracing backend sampled at ten percent under load — which is when the disputed run happened. The span that recorded the human approval was one of the ninety percent dropped. Nothing was broken; the system behaved exactly as configured, and the configuration had been chosen for a debugging tool because nobody had asked it to be evidence.

Fix. Approvals and effectful tool calls moved to an append-only record written synchronously before dispatch, with traces left sampled for everything else. Applying it late meant that for the disputed period there was no reconstruction available — the outcome was visible in the downstream system and the authorisation was not, so the dispute was settled on the customer's account rather than on the facts.

10. 🔗 Connections

⬆️ Depends on (concepts assumed)

  • auditability and traceability — what a trail captures.

🔁 Decides / constrains (other decisions this one forces)

  • §11 Where the approval gate sits — the approval record is the part that must be evidence.

  • §11 Isolation by filter or by construction — traces are the fourth surface people forget to scope.

  • §7 What happens to the effects a failed run already caused — record-before-effect is the same ordering as the outbox.

  • §12 Eval and observability — the trace half of this split lives there.

🏗️ Design problems that hinge on this

  • §14 Support agent that takes actions — a disputed refund is exactly this note's failure story.

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • The disclosure class a missed tenant key produces — OWASP LLM02:2025 Sensitive Information Disclosure

  • Per-tenant retrieval and access control in the index — OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025

0. 🔒 Owned Elsewhere

Concepts assumed (don't re-read unless rusty):

  • Access Control & Security — Per-Tenant Retrieval — per-tenant retrieval and filtering.

  • Rate limiting quota & API-level multi-tenancy — tenancy at the API layer.

What this note adds: the surface count and the enforcement fork. An agent has four places tenant data accumulates — memory, tool credentials, traces and caches — and the last two are the ones nobody scopes, because they were added as infrastructure rather than as data.

1. 🎯 Recall Check

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
The four surfaces? Memory, tool credentials, traces, caches.
Filter versus construction? A where clause you can forget, versus a namespace you can't.
The surface teams miss? Caches — added for latency, never reviewed as storage.

2. The Decision in 30 Seconds

Isolation by filter means every query carries a tenant predicate and correctness depends on nobody forgetting one; isolation by construction means the tenant is part of the address — a namespace, a separate index, a credential that can only see one tenant — so a forgotten key fails rather than leaks. I default to construction for credentials and memory, because those are the surfaces where a miss is a disclosure, and I accept filtering only where a single miss is recoverable. The part worth saying out loud is that there are four surfaces, not one: caches and traces hold tenant data just as memory does, and both are usually introduced by someone solving a latency or debugging problem rather than a data one.

3. 🔱 The Fork

Option Choose when What it costs you Tell-tale signal
Filter (tenant predicate) Single surface, reviewable query paths. Correctness rests on every path remembering; a miss fails open. One shared store, tenant id passed as a parameter.
Namespace per tenant Memory, vector indexes, caches. The default. Per-tenant provisioning, and lifecycle when a tenant leaves. Shared indexes where a filter is the only boundary.
Credential per tenant Tool access and anything downstream. Minting and rotation per tenant. One credential serving every tenant's tool calls.
Separate deployment Regulatory or a single very large customer. Cost and operational multiplicity. Contractual isolation requirements.

4. 📐 What It Flips

If you choose Architecture changes Budget changes Ops changes
Filter None. Cheapest. Every new query path is a chance to leak; review can't scale with it.
Namespace A tenant-derived key in every store's address. Some overhead per namespace. Miss the key and the lookup fails — a bug, not a breach.
Credential per tenant A minting or vault layer between agent and tool. Rotation work. Blast radius of a leak is one tenant.
Separate deployment Everything, once per tenant. Highest. Strongest story, and an upgrade fleet to manage.

The four surfaces, and the failure each produces. Memory — one tenant's summary recalled in another's run. Tool credentials — a call made with the wrong tenant's authority, which the downstream system will honour. Traces — a shared dashboard exposing content across tenants. Caches — a prefix, tool-result or semantic cache keyed without the tenant, serving one customer's answer to another.

Why the cache is the recurring one. It's introduced for latency, reviewed as infrastructure, and keyed for hit rate — the exact pressure that leaves the tenant out, since including it lowers the rate. Same class of bug as a missing WHERE tenant_id, in a component no data-access review covers.

Why construction beats filtering, in one line. A filter is a predicate the caller must remember; a namespace is part of the address the caller cannot omit. The first fails open on a mistake, the second fails closed — and at any real number of query paths, someone makes the mistake.

7. 💥 Failure Story

Symptom. "One customer's document titles appeared in another customer's answer."

Root cause. Retrieval was correctly filtered by tenant; that path had been reviewed carefully. The leak came from a semantic cache added later to cut cost, keyed on the question's embedding alone. Two customers in the same industry asked near-identical questions, the second hit the first's cached answer, and it cited the first customer's documents. Every access control worked — the cache sat in front of all of them.

Fix. The cache key gained the tenant, which cut the hit rate as expected and made the cache correct. The wider fix was a rule that any new store touching request data declares its tenant key in review, so the question is asked when a component is added rather than when it leaks. The late cost was notification: the cache had no per-entry attribution, so establishing which answers had crossed tenants required replaying a month of traffic against the cache contents.

10. 🔗 Connections

⬆️ Depends on (concepts assumed)

  • Access Control & Security — Per-Tenant Retrieval — per-tenant retrieval.

  • Rate limiting quota & API-level multi-tenancy — tenancy at the API layer.

🔁 Decides / constrains (other decisions this one forces)

  • §11 Whose authority the tool call runs with — per-tenant credentials are this note's strongest form.

  • §11 Whether the audit trail is logging or a record of decision — traces are the third surface.

  • §10 Which cache tier, and where each one stops being safe — the fourth surface, priced there.

  • §5 Which store holds this piece of state — every store this names needs a tenant key.

🏗️ Design problems that hinge on this

  • §14 Multi-tenant agent platform — the four surfaces are the design review.

📚 Reference Links

  • The list itself, 2025 edition — OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025

  • The agentic extension, which is the part that applies to tool-using systems — OWASP: agentic AI threats and mitigations

0. 🔒 Owned Elsewhere

Concepts assumed (don't re-read unless rusty):

  • owasp and agentic threat modeling — the entries and the threat-modelling frameworks.

What this note adds: what it's for in a round. The Top 10 is a coverage check, not a design — naming it proves reading; walking a design against it proves engineering.

1. 🎯 Recall Check

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
What it's good for? Checking nothing was forgotten, after the design exists.
What it isn't? An architecture. It names risks, not resolutions.
The entries an agent touches most? LLM01 injection, LLM02 disclosure, LLM06 excessive agency, LLM10 unbounded consumption.

2. The Decision in 30 Seconds

I use it at the end, as a sweep. The design comes from the forks — which trifecta leg is broken, whose credential the call runs with, where the gate sits — and the Top 10 is then the list I walk to find what I didn't think about. Citing it early is a tell: it signals reading and decides nothing, because every entry names a risk and none names a resolution. For a tool-using system the agentic extension is the more useful document.

3. 🔱 The Fork

Option Choose when What it costs you Tell-tale signal
Cite it as framing Opening a security conversation with a non-specialist. Nothing, and it decides nothing. Answering "how is this secure" with a list of risk names.
Run it as a coverage sweep After the design exists. The useful mode. Ten questions' worth of time, most already answered. A finished design nobody has checked for gaps.
Threat-model the agent directly Novel topology, or high stakes. Real effort — enumerate assets, entry points, effects. A system the generic list doesn't describe well.
